newsitem.title: CHINA: Britain will not turn back on HK-in-China--Cook.
newsitem.headline: Britain will not turn back on HK-in-China--Cook.

text.p: Foreign Secretary Robin Cook pledged on Tuesday that Britain would not turn its back on Hong Kong and told citizens after their handover to China :"We will walk with you".

Cook told a news conference after the transfer-of-power ceremonies that he will return to Hong Kong at the end of the year and also visit Beijing "to make sure that our relations with both are strong".
Cook, who attended the handover with Britain's Prime Minister Tony Blair, said he had won two important concessions from Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.

"Chinese troops should not be seen in marches or in armoured personnel carriers on the streets of Hong Kong," he told reporters on the day that several thousand members of the People's Liberation Army swept in by sea, air and armoured convoy.
Cook said he had also won assurances that elections would be held in Hong Kong by next May.
"We will monitor them closely to satisfy ourselves that those elections are really free and fair," he said.

The watering down of Hong Kong's civil rights and democracy was fiercely opposed by Britain and by Hong Kong's own democracy movement which won 70 percent of the directly elected seats in the legislature in a vote held two years ago.
China has replaced the body with a provisional legislature handpicked by Beijing.
China has sent about 5,000 People's Liberation Army troops into Hong Kong where memories are still vivid of Beijing's 1989 Tiananmen massacre of unarmed demonstrators by troops.
"Britain cannot turn its back on Hong Kong and will not," Cook said.
He said that if China did not fulfill its pledge to hold elections within a year "then certainly the United Nations is one useful forum in which we can explore that breach of the declaration".
The 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration gave Hong Kong 50 years of autonomy under Beijing's "one country, two systems" formula.
"The message I leave with the people of Hong Kong is that we will walk with you through the 50 years for which terms of the handover remain in legal force," he said.

Cook said he was flying back to Britain feeling that there were more pluses than minuses in the handover. He said he felt more encouraged about the future, particularly after he and Blair met Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
But he did single out one big minus -- the dismissal of the elected legislative council -- and he praised leading Democrat Martin Lee for what he called a mature and restrained protest.
"Britain will continue to recognise him as the leader of the largest single party in Hong Kong and to meet with him to hear their views," he said.
